title: What Technical Debt Would You Knowingly Take On to Hit This Deadline?
summary: Tests whether you can name a specific, deliberate corner cut and describe how you'd track and repay it — distinct from scope-cutting, which trims features rather than incurring debt inside a feature you still ship.

slides.markdown:
The interviewer asks: **"what technical debt would you knowingly take on to hit this deadline?"** This differs from cutting scope — here you're shipping the full feature, but with an intentionally worse implementation underneath.

A strong answer names a specific implementation shortcut, states explicitly why it's safe to take now, and says what would trigger paying it back later.

Ask whether the pressure is a one-time deadline or an ongoing pace that would make this debt compound indefinitely if never repaid. Which corner, if cut, is genuinely reversible later versus one that gets more expensive to fix the longer it's live?

The second question is the crux: some shortcuts stay isolated and cheap to fix whenever you get to them; others actively get worse the longer they're in production, and those need a much tighter leash.

Name a specific implementation shortcut, state explicitly why it's safe to take *now*, and say what would trigger paying it back.

All three parts matter — a shortcut without a stated trigger is indistinguishable from debt no one ever intends to repay, and a shortcut without a "why it's safe now" is just building it badly with an excuse attached after the fact.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: hardcoding a single-region deployment
slides.markdown:
A worked example: hardcoding a single-region deployment to hit launch instead of building multi-region from day one, explicitly because the business's initial user base is entirely in one geography. The trigger is a clear one — international expansion plans — rather than an open-ended "we'll get to it."

This debt is safe now because the missing capability (multi-region) has no current user impact — the geography that would need it doesn't exist yet as a customer base.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: synchronous polling instead of event-driven
slides.markdown:
A concrete scenario: a team ships a feature using synchronous polling instead of the properly event-driven design they eventually want, because building the event infrastructure would blow the deadline. They explicitly log this as debt with a follow-up ticket, and revisit it once polling load actually becomes a measurable cost — rather than replacing it preemptively or forgetting about it.

The trigger here is measurable and specific (polling load crossing a threshold), which is what makes this a managed piece of debt rather than a permanent shortcut disguised as a temporary one.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: debt that's never safe to take on
slides.markdown:
![Debt that's safe to defer has a shrinking fix cost over time; debt that isn't has a growing one](assets/debt-cost-over-time.svg)

Skipping data-integrity safeguards — for example, no idempotency key on a payment write — is debt that gets more expensive and riskier the longer it's live, not less, and shouldn't be on the "acceptable to defer" list regardless of the deadline.

The distinguishing test: does the cost of fixing this shrink or grow the longer it's live in production? Debt that grows is a correctness or safety issue, not a legitimate shortcut.

assets.alt: Debt that's safe to defer has a shrinking fix cost over time; debt that isn't has a growing one

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Technical debt is a legitimate tool, not automatically a mistake. The difference between good and bad debt is whether it's named, tracked, and has a clear repayment trigger, versus silent and indefinite.

Good debt is a deliberate, visible trade you can point to and justify. Bad debt is indistinguishable, from the outside, from simply having built the thing poorly with no intention of ever fixing it.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: making sure the debt actually gets paid down
slides.markdown:
Follow-up: "how do you make sure this debt actually gets paid down instead of becoming permanent?" The same discipline as deferred scope: a tracked ticket with an owner and a concrete trigger condition, revisited at a regular cadence — every planning cycle, for instance — not a mental note that quietly disappears.

Without a regular revisit cadence, even a well-tracked ticket can sit untouched indefinitely — the cadence is what actually forces the question back onto the table.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: where's the line under more pressure to stack debt
slides.markdown:
Follow-up: "the deadline moved up again and there's pressure to take on more debt in the same area — where's the line?" The line is whatever debt compounds or touches correctness or safety. Debt that stays isolated and doesn't get more expensive to fix over time is more acceptable to stack than debt that does.

This reuses the same growing-cost test from the "never safe" slide — it's the consistent filter for every additional debt decision, not a one-time judgment call made only at the original deadline.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: vague debt with no repayment plan
slides.markdown:
**Wrong move:** describing "we'd take on some technical debt" with no specific corner named and no repayment plan.

**Why it's wrong:** this is indistinguishable from just building it badly with no intention of ever fixing it — the value of naming debt explicitly is entirely in the specificity and the trigger, and a vague statement has neither.

**Correct model:** always name the exact shortcut and the exact condition that would trigger revisiting it.

Name a specific implementation shortcut — not a vague "we'd take on some debt" — state why it's safe to take now, and name the concrete trigger that would prompt paying it back. Track it as an owned ticket revisited on a regular cadence, since untracked debt tends to become permanent.

Never put correctness or safety on the acceptable-to-defer list — debt is only legitimate where the cost of fixing it stays flat or shrinks over time, not where it compounds the longer it's live.
